partner_context.their_ambition: The western Indian Ocean — Seychelles, Mauritius and Zanzibar — is one of the world's great luxury-island regions, built on getting affluent guests from the airport to a private island or reef resort.
partner_context.their_pressure: Transfers are the weak link: rough diesel speedboats, weather-limited helicopters and small inter-island planes, all carbon-heavy and threatening the fragile reefs these economies depend on. As resorts decarbonize and reefs come under protection, the legacy transfer fleet is the bottleneck.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier turns the transfer layer into a fast, smooth, all-weather, zero-emission, low-wake foiling network — protecting the reefs while transforming the guest experience, with the live Maldives network as the proof case next door.

hero.title: Navier × Indian Ocean — luxury island-hopping, reef-safe
hero.subtitle: Re-platforming Seychelles, Mauritius and Zanzibar transfers on foiling-electric vessels.
hero.what_we_do_together: Navier brings a software-defined foiling-electric fleet that replaces rough diesel transfers and weather-bound air legs with fast, silent, low-wake island-hopping across the western Indian Ocean. The partnership pairs Navier's platform, captain training and certification path with regional resort relationships and island-by-island rollout — applying the live Maldives playbook to its sister archipelagos.

why_now: The Maldives network — ~100 vessels, $100M, phasing now — proved foiling-electric works at archipelago scale (WSJ + Bloomberg, May 2026). Seychelles, Mauritius and Zanzibar are the natural next clusters: same premium transfer demand, same reef-protection imperative, same weather-limited legacy fleet — and the proof case is already operating in the same ocean.
multimodal_fit: Navier slots between the international airport and the resort jetty — Mahé to the inner-island resorts, Mauritius to its lagoon resorts and Île aux Cerfs, Zanzibar's Stone Town to the northern beaches and Mnemba. Foiling takes the high-value near and mid legs; helicopters and inter-island planes keep only the longest outer hops.

proof_points.claim: The proof case is live in the same ocean.
The platform is proven in service.
proof_points.evidence: 10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out.

proof_points.claim: Premium transfer demand is large and growing.
proof_points.evidence: Seychelles, Mauritius and Zanzibar together draw millions of high-spend visitors a year, nearly all needing a sea or air transfer.

proof_points.claim: Reef protection favours low-wake zero-emission vessels.
proof_points.evidence: Mnemba and Seychelles marine parks restrict high-impact craft — foiling's low wake and zero emissions align with conservation mandates.

proof_points.claim: Foiling is built for protected reefs.
proof_points.evidence: Seychelles (Ste Anne, Curieuse, Aldabra) and Zanzibar (Mnemba) marine parks restrict high-wake craft; a near-silent, zero-wake, zero-emission foil is conservation-aligned by design.

objections.concern: Can it handle open Indian Ocean crossings?
objections.response: The foil flies above the chop for a smoother ride than a diesel speedboat. Pioneer II covers intra-island and resort legs all-electric; Quanta-LR hybrid handles the longer crossings (e.g. Dar↔Zanzibar) with no charging at small island jetties.

objections.concern: What about charging at remote island resorts?
objections.response: Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at resort jetties; Quanta-LR needs no charging at all — removing the constraint that kept electric out of the outer islands.

objections.concern: Does it replace planes and helicopters?
objections.response: No — it complements them. Foiling takes the high-frequency near and mid legs (all-weather, after-dark, lower cost); air keeps the longest outer hops. Together they improve network reliability.

objections.concern: Is it deliverable across three countries?
objections.response: Yes — phased cluster-by-cluster (Seychelles → Mauritius → Zanzibar), each anchored on its airport hub, applying the proven Maldives rollout playbook.

close.title: The Maldives playbook, ocean-wide.
close.body: Foiling-electric island-hopping is already live in the Indian Ocean. Seychelles, Mauritius and Zanzibar are the natural next clusters — same demand, same reefs to protect, same proof case operating next door.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop - roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists - the open water and the berths and jetties already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces just converged: the technology crossed from prototype to platform (10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out), decarbonization mandates turned legacy diesel fleets into stranded liabilities, and the hybrid removed the 'no charging' excuse. The marine layer is being claimed cluster-by-cluster right now.
why_navier_now.n35_note: Resort arrivals run on the N35 Shuttle — 12–15 guests plus luggage, level dockside boarding, an all-weather enclosed cabin and a shallow 1.5 ft draft for lagoon and reef-flat approaches; the low-wake foil is gentle on the marine parks these islands depend on.
